  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem

Vignette:
Dr. John Lee, a 63-year-old American male and accomplished doctor, has been navigating the aftermath of an encounter with terrorism that occurred several months ago. The traumatic event unfolded during his routine commute on a crowded city bus when it was targeted by a group of terrorists. Dr. Lee vividly remembers the chaos as he heard violent exchanges, commands barked in authoritative tones, and the general pandemonium that ensued. The fear and helplessness he experienced were overwhelming. In the weeks following this event, Dr. Lee began to notice significant changes in his behavior and mindset. He became acutely aware of any sounds that might suggest someone was breaking into his home. Even inside his own house, he felt a constant sense of unease and remained on high alert, constantly scanning for potential threats. This hypervigilance had seeped into other areas of his life as well; Dr. Lee found himself becoming irritable and snapping at colleagues and family members more frequently than before. The trauma had fundamentally altered Dr. Lee’s perception of the world around him. He now firmly believed that his life had been irreparably damaged by this event, leaving him feeling like everything he once knew was lost. The world seemed far more dangerous to him now; every encounter with strangers or authority figures felt fraught with hidden danger and deceit. This distrust extended even to those close to him, making it difficult for Dr. Lee to relax in social situations or feel truly safe. His avoidance behaviors began to manifest early on. He refused to ride the bus again, opting instead for longer drives that added significant time to his daily commute. The stress of avoiding public transport had taken a toll on his schedule and energy levels, making it challenging for him to maintain his usual work pace. His irritability also affected his interactions with patients; he found himself less patient and more terse during consultations, which led to some strained relationships with colleagues who noticed the change in his demeanor. Dr. Lee’s marriage has also been impacted by these changes. He often isolates himself from family activities, preferring to stay home where he feels safer, even though this means missing out on shared experiences with his wife and children. His wife has expressed concern about his increased isolation and irritability but Dr. Lee struggles to articulate the depth of his fears. Despite these challenges, what finally prompted Dr. Lee to seek help was a particularly tense interaction at work where he lashed out at a nurse over a minor issue, leading to an uncomfortable meeting with HR. The realization that his behavior was beginning to affect his professional life and personal relationships made him acutely aware of the need for intervention. In therapy, Dr. Lee hopes to regain control over his reactions and restore some semblance of normalcy in his daily life. His primary fear is that he will never feel safe again or fully trust others, but deep down, he also harbors a hope that through understanding and support, he can find a way to reconcile his trauma and rebuild a sense of security and connection with the world around him.
